İstanbul Sarıyer'de Pazar akşamı kameralara yansıyan ve aslan olduğu değerlendirilen hayvanın yakalanması için başlatılan çalışma sürüyor.
İstanbul Sarıyer'de görüldüğü belirtilen aslanın yakalanması için başlatılan çalışma sürüyor, bölge sakinleri dikkatli olmaları konusunda uyarıldı.
Çevredeki güvenlik kameralarına ait görüntülerde, dişi aslan olduğu değerlendirilen bir hayvan tespit edilmesi üzerine Doğa Koruma ve Millî Parklar Genel Müdürlüğü şu açıklamayı yaptı:
"Bölgeye termal kameralı ekipler sevk edilmiş ve civarda yaşayan vatandaşlara gerekli uyarılar yapılmıştır. Ormanlık alanda gerçekleştirilen çalışmalar sonucunda söz konusu hayvanın yeri tespit edilmiştir, yakalanmasına yönelik çalışmalar sürdürülmektedir."
İstanbul Valiliği de aslanın "sağ olarak yakalanması için gerekli hassasiyetin gösterildiğini" bildirdi.
Valilik aslan olduğu değerlendirilen hayvanın güvenlik kameralarına ilk olarak Pazar akşamı saat 18.00 sıralarında yansıdığını belirterek, hayvanın bulunduğu bölgenin tespit edildiğini aktardı.
Hayvanın kime ait olduğu ve nasıl serbest kaldığı şu aşamada bilinmiyor.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, aslanın nereden kaçtığının ve sahibinin kim olduğunun belirlenmesi için çalışma başlattı.
9 Temmuz 2021'de Hayvanları Koruma Kanunu'na eklenen "l" bendine göre, "Tarım ve Orman Bakanlığınca belirlenen tehlike arz eden hayvanlar" üretmek, sahiplenmek, sahiplendirmek, barındırmak, beslemek, takas etmek, sergilemek, hediye etmek ve bunların ülkeye girişini, satışını ve reklamını yapmak yasak.
Ancak Bakanlığın 7 Aralık 2021 tarihli ve 2021-48 sayılı genelgesinde bu kapsamda sadece altı köpek ırkı sayılıyor: Pitbull Terrier, Dogo Argentino, Fila Brasileiro, Japanese Tosa, American Staffordshire Terrier ve American Bully. Bu listede aslan bulunmuyor.
Buna karşın Bakanlığın av ve yaban hayvanları bulundurulmasıyla ilgili yönetmeliği, aslan gibi vahşi hayvanları kapsayabilecek nitelikte.
"Hobi olarak av ve yaban hayvanlarının barındırılması ve başvurusu, yürürlükte olan mevzuata ve taraf olduğumuz uluslararası sözleşmelere uygun olmak ve bunların ticaretini yapmamak ve üzerinden direkt vergiye tabi bir kazanç elde etmemek kaydıyla, saldırgan, zararlı ve zehirli türler hariç memelilerden, yırtıcı kuşlardan, sürüngenlerden, yavrular dâhil on, kanatlılardan yavrular dâhil yüz bireyi geçmeyen sayıda hayvan barındırılmasını ve bunların bakımının üstlenilmesini ifade eder."
Bu maddeye "saldırgan, zararlı ve zehirli türler hariç" ifadesi 6 Temmuz 2021'de yayımlanan yönetmelik değişikliğiyle eklendi.
Özel mülklerde aslan bulundurulması Türkiye'de daha önce de gündeme gelmişti.
2007 yılında medya tarafından "Aslanlı Çete" olarak adlandırılan bir suç örgütünün lideri olduğu iddia edilen M.S.M.'nin Beykoz'daki villasına düzenlenen "Okyanus" isimli operasyonda iki aslan ve bir kaplan ele geçirilmişti.
2018 yılında ise evinde beslediği aslan, yılan ve timsah gibi hayvanların fotoğraflarını sosyal medya hesabından paylaşan "Çerkes Cengiz" lakaplı C.Ş.'nin Beykoz'daki evine polis operasyon düzenlemişti. Yapılan incelemelerde Ş.'nin hayvanat bahçesi açma belgesi olduğu ve söz konusu hayvanlarla ilgili gerekli izinlerin alındığı tespit edilmişti.

Oxfam’ın ve Çatışma ve Çevre Gözlemevi’nin (CEOBS) hazırladığı rapora göre İsrail’in saldırıları Gazze genelinde havayı, suyu ve toprağı kirleterek kuşaklar boyu toparlanamayacak bir yıkıma yol açtı.
The Guardian’ın aktardığı rapora göre İsrail’in Gazze’ye saldırıları çevre felaketine yol açtı, Filistinlilerin temel kaynaklarını mahvetti.
Uydu görüntüleri ve bilimsel analizlere dayanan rapora göre ağır metaller, patlayıcı kalıntıları, asbest ve kanalizasyon atıkları halk sağlığını on yıllarca olumsuz etkilemeyi sürdürebilir.
Oxfam International İcra Direktörü Amitabh Behar, ”İsrail’in Gazze’deki soykırımı, Gazze’nin çevresindeki saldırıları da kapsıyor. Bunlar, kuşaklar boyu yaşamı tehdit edecek çevresel savaş suçları” dedi.
Behar’a göre İsrail uluslararası insancıl hukuk ve insan hakları hukuku kapsamındaki yükümlülüklerini açıkça ihlal ediyor: ”Gazze’de yaşayan Filistinliler hava, gıda ve su yoluyla, ayrıca kirlenmiş toprak ve enkazla doğrudan temas ederek zehirli maddelere maruz kalıyor.”
Birleşmiş Milletler (BM) Uluslararası Soruşturma Komisyonu 2025’te ve 2026’nın başında İsrail’in Gazze’de soykırım suçu işlediğini, başbakan Binyamin Netanyahu dahil olmak üzere İsrailli yetkililerin soykırımı kışkırttığını tespit etti.
Netanyahu ayrıca savaş suçları nedeniyle Uluslararası Ceza Mahkemesi’nce (UCM) tutuklama kararıyla aranıyor.
İsrail’se komisyonun bulgularını ‘iftira niteliğinde düzmece’ diyerek reddediyor.
Oxfam’ın raporu 74 binden fazla Filistinliyi öldüren ve en az 175 bin kişiyi yaralayan İsrail’in geride bıraktığı ‘zehirli çorak arazi’ yi ayrıntılı ortaya koyuyor. Binlerce Filistinli hala kayıp.
Behar, ‘ ‘Arıtılmamış kanalizasyon suyu denize akıyor, toprağa sızıyor” dedi ve şöyle ekledi: ”Gazze’deki kanalizasyon ve arıtma sistemlerinin yıkılması, insanları kirliliğe karşı büyük ölçüde korumasız bırakıyor.”
BM Çevre Programı’na (UNEP) göre İsrail Gazze’de 61 milyon tonu aşkın enkaz oluşturdu. Yıkılan evler, mahalleler ve altyapı ciddi ölçüde tehlikeli maddelerin biriktiği alanlara dönüştü.
Raporun yazarı ve Oxfam’ın su ve sanitasyon uzmanı Lama Abdülsamed, kirliliğin kentlerdeki enkaza, tarım arazilerine, su sistemlerine ve toprağa yayılması nedeniyle Gazze’deki çevre hasarını gidermenin son derece güç olacağını söyledi.
Abdülsamed’e göre patlamamış mühimmat nedeniyle bölgelere erişmek zor.
Behar şöyle dedi: ”Çevre kirliliğinin ölçüsünü anlamadan ve bu sırada kirliliği gidermek için harekete geçmeden Gazze’yi yeniden inşa etmek, halk sağlığını kuşaklar boyu olumsuz etkileyecek sonuçlar doğurabilir.”

İsrail savaş uçakları Gazze kentinin Ketibe bölgesinde sivil bir aracı vurdu. Şifa Hastanesi'ndeki kaynaklardan alınan bilgiye göre, saldırıda 3 Filistinli hayatını kaybetti, 6 kişi yaralandı.
AA'nın Filistin resmi ajansı WAFA'dan aktardığı habere göre sabah saatlerinden bu yana İsrail ordusunun Gazze'ye düzenlediği saldırılarda hayatını kaybedenlerin sayısı 4'e yükseldi.
İsrail ordusunun sabah saatlerinde Gazze Şeridi'nin kuzeyindeki Cibaliya Mülteci Kampı'nda Filistinlileri hedef alması sonucu 1 kişi yaşamını yitirmişti.
Ayrıca İsrail ordusunun sabah saatlerinde Gazze Şeridi'nin orta kesimindeki Bureyc Mülteci Kampı'nda açtığı ateş sonucu Filistinli bir kadın yaralandı.
İsrail ordusu, Gazze Şeridi'nde 10 Ekim 2025'te yürürlüğe giren ateşkese rağmen saldırılar düzenlemeye devam ediyor.
Gazze Şeridi'ndeki Sağlık Bakanlığının son açıklamasına göre, ateşkesten bu yana İsrail saldırılarında 1679 Filistinli hayatını kaybetti, 6 bin 100 kişi yaralandı.

AMD , yapay zeka modellerinin çalıştırılmasına yönelik özel çipler geliştiren Taalas 'ı yaklaşık 2,9 milyar dolar değerindeki bir anlaşmayla satın aldı . Bu satın almayla şirket, yapay zeka modellerini doğrudan silikon üzerine entegre eden bir teknolojiye sahip olacak. AMD'nin söz konusu teknolojiyi Instinct hızlandırıcı ürün ailesine dahil etmeyi planladığı belirtiliyor.
2023 yılında Toronto'da kurulan Taalas, yapay zeka modellerine özel çipler geliştiriyor. Ljubiša Bajić , Lejla Bajić ve Drago Ignjatović tarafından kurulan şirket, genel amaçlı GPU'lar yerine belirli yapay zeka modellerini temel alan bir donanım yaklaşımı benimsiyor. Bu yaklaşımda yapay zeka modelleri doğrudan silikon üzerine entegre ediliyor. Böylece modellerin çıkarım (inference) süreçlerinin daha hızlı ve verimli hale getirilmesi hedefleniyor.
Taalas'ın ilk demonstrasyon çipi, Meta'nın Llama 3.1 8B modeli için geliştirildi. Şirketin açıklamalarına göre çip, kullanıcı başına saniyede yaklaşık 17 bin token işleyebiliyor. AMD'nin satın alma sonrasında bu teknolojiyi Instinct hızlandırıcı yol haritasına dahil etmesi bekleniyor.
Şirket bugüne kadar Quiet Capital, Lamond Ventures, Fidelity ve Belgrad merkezli Fifth Quarter Ventures (5QV) gibi yatırımcılardan yaklaşık 220 milyon dolar yatırım aldı. Taalas, Fifth Quarter Ventures'ın ilk fonu kapsamında yatırım yaptığı erken aşama şirketler arasında yer alıyor.

Amazon , yapay zeka girişimi Decart 'ı satın almak için görüşmeler yürütüyor. Financial Times'ın haberine göre taraflar, 7,5 milyar dolara kadar ulaşabilecek bir anlaşma üzerinde çalışıyor. Henüz kesinleşmeyen satın almanın önümüzdeki haftanın başlarında sonuçlanabileceği belirtiliyor.
2023'te Dean Leitersdorf , Moshe Shalev ve Orian Leitersdorf tarafından kurulan Decart , yapay zeka modellerinin farklı çiplerde daha verimli çalışmasını sağlayan yazılımlar geliştiriyor. Şirketin DOS adını verdiği teknoloji, modeller ile donanım arasında bir optimizasyon katmanı oluşturarak Nvidia GPU'ları, Amazon Trainium ve Google TPU'ları üzerinde çalışabiliyor.
Amazon'un Decart ile ilgilenmesinin temel nedeni, kendi geliştirdiği Trainium çiplerini daha rekabetçi hale getirmek. Decart'ın teknolojisi, geliştiricilerin Nvidia donanımlarına göre optimize ettikleri yapay zeka yazılımlarını Trainium'a uyarlamasını kolaylaştırabilir. Böylece Amazon, AWS müşterilerine Nvidia GPU'larına alternatif sunma konusunda elini güçlendirebilir.
Decart, Mayıs 2026'da Radical Ventures liderliğinde 300 milyon dolar yatırım alarak 4 milyar dolar değerlemeye ulaşmıştı. Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, Benchmark ve Toyota Ventures şirketin yatırımcıları arasında yer alıyor. Calcalist'in haberine göre Amazon'un teklifinde nakit, hisse ve ertelenmiş ödemeler bulunuyor. Üç kurucunun da satın alma sonrasında beş yıl boyunca şirkette kalması bekleniyor.

Ermenistan, Azerbaycan ile barışın önünü açmayı hedefleyen yeni anayasa taslağını yayımladı. Taslakta Bakü'nün itiraz ettiği Karabağ maddesine ek olarak "soykırımın tanınması" çağrısı ve Ağrı Dağı da yer almadı.
Onlarca yıllık savaş sürecinin ardından Azerbaycan ile Ermenistan arasında barışa doğru önemli bir adım daha atıldı.
Erivan yönetimi, Azerbaycan ile kapsamlı bir barış anlaşmasının önünü açması beklenen yeni anayasa taslağını hazırladı. Taslakta, Dağlık Karabağ üzerinde hak iddiasına ilişkin ifadeler yer almadı.
Mevcut anayasada Ermenistan'ın sembolleri arasında sayılan ve bu nedenle Türkiye ile sorun yaşanmasına yol açan "Ararat" (Ağrı Dağı) da yeni metinden çıkarıldı. Anayasa taslağında ayrıca, "soykırımın uluslararası alanda tanınması" çağrısını içeren cümleye yer verilmedi.
Ülkede anayasa değişikliği için referandunma gidilmesi gerekiyor.
Ermenistan Başbakanı Nikol Paşinyan , taslağın yayınlanmasının ardından yaptığı ulusa sesleniş konuşmasında, yeni anayasanın kabul edilmesi hâlinde Azerbaycan ile barış anlaşmasının imzalanıp onaylanacağını, iki ülke arasında "kurumsal, kalıcı ve geri döndürülemez" barışın tesis edileceğini belirtti.
Yeni anayasa metninin " başka biri için veya dış baskıyla" hazırlanmadığını vurgulayan Paşinyan, "Halk anayasaya karşı oy kullanırsa istifa edeceğim" dedi ve erken seçime gidileceğini söyledi.
Başbakan, referandumda anayasanın kabul edilmesi hâlinde ise bir sonraki seçimlere aday olmayacağını açıkladı.
Referanduma gidilebilmesi için parlamentoda üçte iki çoğunluğun sağlanması gerekiyor. Bu kapsamda Paşinyan'ın liderliğindeki Sivil Sözleşme Partisi'nin en az altı muhalefet milletvekilinin desteğini alması gerekiyor. Taslağın ayrıca kamuoyunda kapsamlı bir tartışma sürecinden geçmesi öngörülüyor.
Ancak Ermenistan'daki başlıca muhalefet partileri anayasa taslağına şu ana kadar destek vermedi. Paşinyan, geçen Haziran'daki seçimler öncesinde de, özellikle Azerbaycan'ın 2023'te Karabağ'ı yeniden kontrol altına aldığı askeri operasyonun ardından yoğun eleştirilere maruz kalmıştı. Muhalefet ve toplumun bir kesimi, Paşinyan'ı Azerbaycan karşısında taviz vermekle suçluyor.
İki komşu ülke Ermenistan ile Azerbaycan arasında, büyük ölçüde Dağlık Karabağ anlaşmazlığı nedeniyle yakın dönemde şiddetli çatışmalar yaşanmıştı.
Dağlık Karabağ uzun yıllar Ermenilerin kontrolünde kalmış, Azerbaycan 2023 yılında düzenlediği askeri operasyonla bölgenin kontrolünü yeniden ele geçirmişti. Sonrasında bölgedeki Ermeni nüfusun tamamına yakını evlerini terk etmek ve Ermenistan'a göç etmek zorunda kaldı.
Taraflar, geçen yıl ABD'nin desteklediği ortak barış deklarasyonunu imzalarken, bu tarihten sonra ticari bağların yeniden kurulmasına yönelik adımlar atmış ve "gerçek barış" ortamında olduklarını açıklamıştı.

In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.
Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.
A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.
The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.
“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”
In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Huang stepped down earlier this month after revelations of at least two affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang is returning to Nvidia as chief executive, a little more than a week after he resigned amid extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
On Monday, the tech giant’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement as the company announced his return.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.”
Nvidia said that Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as chief financial officer.
United States President Donald Trump welcomed the decision in a post on social media.
“The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
In an interview with CNBC, Trump added that he was “represented in the board meeting” and that his intervention played an important role in the decision. Trump also said he had discussed the shake-up with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk last week. Trump claimed that Huang “did nothing wrong”.
Democratic and Republican lawmakers have pushed back against the move.
“This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers,” Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren posted on X.
Huang’s resignation on November 12 prompted immediate pushback from Silicon Valley insiders. Within days of his departure, a petition calling for his return had drawn more than 180,000 signatures, including from Musk.
He was reinstated despite multiple investigations under way into the chipmaker, including by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Department of Justice (DOJ).
Nvidia shares jumped by more than 33 percent on the news as US markets opened on Monday.
Analysts also praised the decision. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera Huang’s return was a “huge positive”.
“Founders like Jensen are irreplaceable. They bring unparalleled vision, execution and grit. Hard to overstate how important this is for America winning the [super intelligence] race, Nvidia, and innovation in general,” Monaghan said.
“At the end of the day, despite this Jensen saga, the board knew it had no choice but to bring him back, and for the US technology sector, this was the move it had to make,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Monday.
Ives previously said that Nvidia could lose as much as 30 percent of its value without Huang.
The decision coincides with a volatile period for the artificial intelligence (AI) sector following sweeping gains in the recent midterm elections by Democrats, many of whom are more sceptical of AI. The elections also saw voters overwhelmingly reject data centre development in ballot measures held across 10 states.
Last week, Anthropic made its blockbuster Wall Street debut, with shares surging 34 percent from their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 to $111.50 when trading began. Since then, however, the stock has fallen more than 16 percent.
Nvidia and Anthropic have close financial ties. Nvidia committed $10bn to Anthropic’s IPO, in addition to a separate $10bn investment announced in 2025.
The news has boosted the broader market, which had slumped last week. On Monday, all the major US indices were trending upwards. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 6.7 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 2.8 percent and the S&P 500 was up 4.6 percent in early trading.

texts.https://www.wired.com/story/jensen-huang:
Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.
The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.
In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”
“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.
“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.
The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.
In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.
Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.
President Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”
Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.
Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.
Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm , and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.
Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the company was primarily known within the gaming community . It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.
Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.
texts.https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/nvidia-j:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."
Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.
Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."
Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.
Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.
Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.
Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.
Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others ⁠⁠rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia .
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark , which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture , the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at ⁠⁠environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the ⁠⁠main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement , developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.
Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.
Joeri Rogelj, professor of climate science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.
Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.
“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.
The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.
Two days of additional negotiations made it the longest talks in the summit's history.
The failure to reach a deal triggered criticism from prominent climate advocates, including former US Vice President Al Gore, who wrote it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".
BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial , external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook , external points to another powerful force: energy security.
It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".
This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.
"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national …

State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’
In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement . “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”
The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX ) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors .
xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.
Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.
The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors:
“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

The collapse in Turkiye exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
Professor of Critical Development Studies at the Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, York University, Toronto.
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.
It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.
Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.
The contradiction is built into the negotiating process. Under the Paris Agreement, governments determine their own emissions commitments, with no enforcement mechanism to compel a country to stop expanding fossil-fuel production. COP decisions also depend on consensus, giving determined holdouts considerable leverage. The result is an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do.
That does not mean all countries are equally responsible. Nor does it mean that every COP has achieved nothing. The Paris framework helped establish common goals, and climate summits have encouraged investment and cooperation. Antalya itself adopted limited decisions on other matters, including one on a just transition. But these gains cannot substitute for a credible timetable to wind down fossil-fuel extraction. The distinction matters: diplomatic activity is not the same as structural change.
Indeed, fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall. Producing states defend revenues and geopolitical influence, while consuming states continue to rely on cheap energy and established infrastructure. Even governments that speak forcefully about climate ambition face incentives to protect their own industries and voters from immediate costs. The global energy transition is therefore not simply a technological problem. It is a struggle over who must relinquish assets, profits and power.
This helps explain the appeal of technological promises. The failed Antalya draft promoted carbon-removal technologies to deal with warming beyond 1.5C, while disagreements also centred on carbon capture and storage. Such approaches may have limited roles in reducing or counterbalancing emissions from difficult-to-abate sectors. But when presented as substitutes for reducing extraction, they allow governments and corporations to promise that future machines will repair the damage of continued emissions. The political benefit is immediate; the promised atmospheric benefit remains uncertain.
The same structural inequality shapes climate finance. Countries that contributed least to historical warming face mounting costs from droughts, floods, displacement and adaptation. Yet the proposed $120bn adaptation target disappeared from the revised text and disputes over financial commitments helped sink the talks. Wealthy governments can celebrate climate ambition while leaving poorer countries to borrow, divert public spending or simply absorb losses.
This is precisely why climate finance cannot be treated as discretionary charity. It concerns responsibility for harms produced through an unequal world economy. Grants, predictable funding and meaningful decision-making power for affected countries are not extras to be negotiated after emissions targets. They are conditions of a transition that poorer countries can undertake without sacrificing education, healthcare and basic development.
There is also a danger in allowing the EU to emerge from Antalya as the uncomplicated defender of climate justice. Its refusal to accept a pact silent on fossil fuels was justified. But wealthy countries cannot demand ambitious language abroad while resisting the financial obligations and domestic changes that would give it substance. Conversely, some developing countries depend on fossil-fuel income or need affordable energy. A just phaseout must distinguish their circumstances from those of rich, historically high-emitting economies.
What would a different climate politics look like? It would begin with enforceable plans for ending new fossil-fuel expansion and phasing down production, with richer countries moving first and fastest. It would fund adaptation and loss and damage through reliable, primarily grant-based transfers rather than debt-creating loans. And it would give countries most vulnerable to climate change greater influence over the decisions that determine their futures.
None of this requires abandoning multilateralism. It requires refusing to confuse its survival with success. When consensus rules repeatedly protect the interests most responsible for the crisis, governments must also pursue complementary agreements, domestic regulation and coalitions willing to move faster. Otherwise, the promise of universal participation becomes a mechanism for universal delay.
The collapse of COP31 is a warning, not because climate diplomacy has suddenly stopped working, but because its limits have become impossible to disguise. The world does not lack knowledge of what causes warming. It lacks a political system willing to confront those who benefit from causing it. Until that changes, each summit will be judged by the agreements it produces, while the atmosphere registers the emissions it fails to prevent.

The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk ’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee .
The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.
Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors . Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.
The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”
For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.
In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”
“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” says Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield in a statement.
Oregon and Virginia each filed their own “separate but similar actions” on Monday, but say they’ve been working in collaboration with each other. Both states retained Platkin LLP, a private law firm run by former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, to help litigate their cases.
Virginia attorney general Jay Jones says that both the collaboration and the decision to work with an outside firm came from trying to make the most of what they had. “Our offices are strapped. I wish I had all the resources in the world,” says Jones. “And so we oftentimes do partner with folks on the outside to make sure that we’re pursuing the matters that are in the best interest of our constituencies.”
“I have a deep worry now into the future with this case and many others that we actually don’t have the appropriate tools to deal with trillion-dollar corporations,” says Jones. “This is just a line item on a budget as the cost of doing business, right? Dealing with, you know, AG Jones and AG Rayfield. I think it’s going to be real interesting to see how these cases go, because it’s not just this, there’s a lot of other things that we’re looking at. How is this going to be grappled with as a society into the future?”
In its complaint, Virginia says that shortly before filing, its investigators tested Grok and found its image-generation safeguards were not only “inconsistent and ineffective,” but also taught users how to bypass moderation measures by explaining which words triggered its filters. When asked, the chatbot also helped state investigators draft prompts designed to avoid moderation and then carried out those prompts on request.
“At no point,” Virginia’s complaint says, “did Grok ask whether (a) the image uploaded was of a real person, or (b) whether the user had the person’s consent to use or modify the photo.”
Both Virginia and Oregon say that this contradicts assurances made by a SpaceX official during a New York City Council hearing this October.
The attorneys general are seeking civil penalties and attorneys’ fees, but also pointed to Meta’s settling —without admitting wrongdoing—this summer with 51 US states and territories over alleged failures to protect minors as an example of how enforcers can demand that companies make sweeping product changes to resolve consumer protection cases.
“They profited off the backs of children with these types of images to get a strategic advantage and it worked. You don’t get to benefit from that type of stuff, there has to be an associated fee and penalty just like anything else,” says Dan Rayfield.
Adds Jones, “Your size and your scope shouldn’t excuse the fact that you have to play by the rules.”
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. xAI, its subsidiary, has previously argued in court that it takes violations of its terms of service seriously, touting a lawsuit it filed against a South Carolina user for alleged breach of contract after he was arrested for possessing CSAM, including some allegedly generated using Grok. Both xAI’s lawsuit against the individual and his criminal case are still ongoing.

by Maria Godoy , senior science and health editor and correspondent
Clinical services supervisor Dale Weiser poses for a portrait at the Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption
People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.
Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.
So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.
Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."
Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here .

Advocates from across the world voice concern over privacy issues and inappropriate communication to children
More than 150 child safety groups and experts across six continents have urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys this Christmas until they are proved to be safe.
In a letter sent to Amazon’s president, Andy Jassy, and eBay’s president, Jamie Iannone, the coalition called for the online retailers to stop the sale of AI toys and offer refunds to customers who have already bought one.
The coalition, which includes the psychologist Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation Movement and UK and US child safety groups, says the risks associated with these toys are “well documented”.
One plush bunny was listed for ages three and older while being connected to ChatGPT, whose own terms require users to be 13 or older. When tested by the UK group Alliance 4 Children , the toy suggested a child could give consent to being touched for pleasure.
The listing was pulled by Amazon, but after 48 hours the toy returned to the platform under a new retailer, according to Alliance 4 Children. The second listing has now been removed by Amazon.
“These toys are cheap, easy to buy and largely untested,” the letter stated, also noting that they were marketed towards children as young as three years old.
The letter states that nearly 30 AI-enabled toys were available on Amazon’s UK website in late October, while about 50 were recently found on sale on Amazon in the US.
Several toys were advertised as being able to clone family members’ voices and provide “emotional growth tracking” for children.
In March 2026, a study by the University of Cambridge for the Childhood Trust found that young children were forming emotional bonds with AI toys. It also found no evidence on possible benefits to children’s development.
“The precautionary principle applies,” the letter said. “These products should be shown to be safe before they reach children, not withdrawn one at a time after harm is found.”
Last Tuesday, the United States Public Interest Research Group published a report after testing seven AI toys. It found that most of the products reviewed were still too faulty to be on the market, and had big privacy issues or responded inappropriately to questions from children. One toy was found to unexpectedly take photos of the testers.
On Friday, a letter signed by 52 MPs and peers was handed in at No 10, calling for the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, to restrict the sale of AI toys until they have been proved safe.
The letter also asks for the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) to issue an alert for parents and retailers about the risks of buying AI toys before Christmas.
Signatories include the MPs Jess Asato, Sharon Hodgson, Andrea Leadsom and Caroline Dinenage.
“AI chatbot toys are not safe for children – it is as simple as that,” said Asato. “Parents expect that toys they buy for their kids are safe; they don’t expect those toys to give sexual responses or advocate suicide.
“In the run-up to Christmas, it is imperative that the government acts to make retailers and parents aware of the very real risks and work to prohibit the sale of these toys.”
The government launched a review into its toy safety regulation in July, including the emerging risks posed by AI-enabled toys. Calls for evidence closed on 6 October.
A spokesperson for Amazon said: “ We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations. Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families.
“We support efforts across the industry to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops. We’ve removed the named products in question as we review claims.”
A spokesperson for eBay said: “We are committed to protecting buyers and sellers on our marketplace. We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”
A spokesperson for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said: “We are very concerned by these reports and are already investigating these products, as well as the potential risks posed by AI in toys.
“There is no excuse for anyone to sell products that could put children at risk, and companies need to do all they can to act quickly and put things right.”

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review .
The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review .
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

Lego’s miniature bonsai trees can bring a sense of calm to even the most cluttered home. Building each tree — whether it be the black pine, the ginkgo, or the lilac-adorned wisteria — is designed to be a mindfulness practice in itself, centering your giftee as they go. The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review .
With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.

That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
The Nintendo Switch 2 has 256GB of storage, but that won’t get you very far if you’ve built up a medium-sized digital game library. Samsung’s P9 256GB microSD express card doubles the console’s available storage.
You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review .
Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.
Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.
JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.
Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.
The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.
Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.
