Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.
One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.
Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.
We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.
RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.
Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.
Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.
RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.
RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.
Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.
To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.
We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.
RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks . Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.
RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.
A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.
These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare.
Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols.
Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric , which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.
This is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. If the barista at your neighborhood coffee shop knows your order before you even walk up to the counter, it might be time to consider learning to make that double Americano at home. With today being National Espresso Day and no shortage of espresso machines on sale ahead of Black Friday, that opportunity is particularly apt.
Each deal below is for a machine that a WIRED reviewer has tested and vetted in their own kitchen. If you take advantage of the savings now, your machine may arrive in time for Thanksgiving, allowing you to impress everyone with your post-dinner cappuccino-making skills.
For more deals, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals , as well as early deals at Amazon and Home Depot .
Updated November 23: I’ve added new deals on machines from Diletta, Fellow, and De'Longhi, plus some accessories. I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.
WIRED reviewers have tried and liked a couple of machines from Diletta, a line of Italian-made, classic semiautomatics exclusive to Seattle Coffee Gear, and they’re all on sale today through December 14.
We reviewed the Bello+ in 2024, appreciating the stylish, industrial design (handmade in Milan) and easily maneuverable steam wand. Our reviewer found it a bit finicky, but Seattle Coffee Gear says it does have a programmable pre-infusion for repeatable recipes.
Best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best , the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.
Fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024 , and according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage , the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.
When we tested this machine , we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. It comes in a variety of finishes, but note that Beige is the cheapest of all right now, at only $915 .
This flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing ,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. It has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a new portafilter.
Formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried , with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was easy enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos; I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.
The Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso . The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and new finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.
We appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a bit quirky. Even so, it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.
Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but we liked this semiautomatic as a beginner-friendly option that pulls some solid shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for those features alone.
Former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested Terra Kaffe's newer Demi and said it was perhaps the “dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee,” with just a dial and a button. Right now it's $200 off, or $300 off with a coffee subscription (Terra-Kaffe offers a house blend specifically made for use on its machines). Its bigger sibling, the TK-02, impressed our tester with its convenience, ease of use, front-facing water filter, and milk carafe. Though it didn't come out on top during a blind espresso taste test we did earlier this year , it's still a great-looking machine that's easy to use and is a whopping $400 off (or $500 with a coffee subscription) for Black Friday.
Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription , Atlas Coffee Club, has a new gift option on offer for Black Friday : a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59 . You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.
Former barista and WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell likes this little scale that includes three magnetic add-ons: a platform, a metal dosing cup, and a catch cup that fits directly onto almost any portafilter.
If grounds are sticking to the plastic components of your coffee grinder, Cottell recommends adding this durable, stylish spray bottle to your espresso setup.
Cottell likes situating this mat underneath your espresso setup, as the lip contains spills and the textured portion is great for drying tools post-washing.
Some machines come with a tamper; others don't. If yours doesn’t, Cottell recommends you get this one . The spring-loaded base unloads 15 pounds of force to create a perfectly flat puck inside your portafilter. (A click lets you know when to stop pushing, so it’s great for beginners, too.)

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army . It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.
The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.
Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.
“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.
Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.
Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.
Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.
“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what ?” he says.
The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.
The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.
The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.
In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.
The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.
The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)
Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.
“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”
For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south , it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Messner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.
“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video generation tools. Amazon, which has been so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

Anthropic warned investors that AI might be conscious—but acting accordingly could hurt its business. So what’s the plan?
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.
Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.
This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).
But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.
Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.
You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.
The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences .
But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.
Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”
It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.
Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines . If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.
Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.
But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.
Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics , the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia . Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.
Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.
That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.
“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.
“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.
Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.
Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.
“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.
Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.
Through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.
Niewolny says he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron . The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.

There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg
Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector ( ‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November ) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign , initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech , providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere. At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova , and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl , have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption. Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources. Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies. James White and Nora Söderberg Department of Technology and Society, Lund University

Drone strikes on two Russian vessels near Libyan coast fuels fears of Ukraine war’s spread.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.
“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.
The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.
The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.
The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.
The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.
Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.
Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.
“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.
A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.
In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.
Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Ukraine’s attacks off the coast of Libya, as well as the targeting of Russian cargo vessels in the Baltic Sea, as a “very dangerous trend”.
Peskov warned Ukraine of “painful” consequences. “The Defence Ministry is dealing with this matter, and information will also be provided through the Defence Ministry if deemed appropriate,” he said.
Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.
“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.
The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.
The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.
In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.
In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.
“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.
Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.
“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.
The sinking of the Merkury, commissioned in 2023, would also weaken Russia’s naval capabilities, Muraviev said.
However, the academic warned that the Gulf of Finland was particularly sensitive because of its geography and the proximity of Russian and NATO forces.
“In my personal view, it is an area where a possible clash between Russia and NATO is quite possible,” he said.
Muraviev added that the attacks could have wider implications for global shipping, which is already facing heightened security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
“[The attacks] just add additional risks to marine operators from across the world,” he said.

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.
Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.
In this screen grab from a video provided by the Security Service of Ukraine on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, a Ukrainian Sea Baby suicide drone attacks the Russian navy corvette Merkury near Benghazi, Libya. Security Service of Ukraine/via AP hide caption
Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.
At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.
A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.
Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.
Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.
Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.
Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.
Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.
At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.
Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.
Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.
The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.
A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.
Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
Although the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues, the two leaders did not mention the border dispute in their public remarks
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

Rescuers brave unstable structures in search for missing as DNA needed to identify victims
Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore ⁠through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for ⁠about 30 people ⁠still missing.
Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.
Said Iqbal, ⁠a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died. He said the ​implementation of safety protocols was being ‌assessed and that he ‌would summon the factory’s chief executive.
Preliminary reports indicated the fire might have ‌been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added. The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the national police’s victim identification division.
She said body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.
The blaze had largely been contained on Sunday but firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations on Monday before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.
“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”
He also said the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.
Anxious relatives have waited for news outside the burnt-out factory.
The Banten province governor, Andra Soni, said an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The firm employs about 5,000 people and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market. Its ‌products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.
The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. He said the facility had adequate evacuation routes and fire protection systems that complied with applicable safety standards and were functioning at the time of the fire.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

Nepal’s PM Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first since coming to power in March.
India will provide Nepal with a $1.62bn economic package in the wake of August’s devastating floods in the country, which led to the deaths and disappearances of thousands of people.
The sum announced on Monday is one of its largest-ever relief commitments, and comes as New Delhi boosts ties with its Himalayan neighbour, where it competes with China for influence.
The announcement followed talks between India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah, who is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first bilateral trip abroad since coming to power in March.
“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August,” Modi said, standing alongside Shah in New Delhi. “To support Nepal’s reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees [$1.6bn].”
August’s floods, which scientists say were caused by the effects of climate change, were triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed and a torrent of water and mud flooded down into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions, as well as into China’s Tibet region on August 26. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 5,000 remain missing.
In October, the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund set aside a sum of $20m for aid to Nepal.
India’s package will include a $377m grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, and a $1.24bn line of credit for energy projects, the countries said in a joint statement.
India is Nepal’s largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60 percent of its imports, worth $8.6bn, while China accounts for 13 percent, or $1.8bn, according to World Bank figures.
Besides the flood relief package, the pair agreed on further cooperation in education and research, satellite communications, and sustainable urban development. The two leaders also jointly opened a train link connecting the countries.
“May the friendship between Nepal and India be one where trust stands as tall as the Himalayas,” said Shah.

At least 24 people were killed in a deadly fire that ripped through a factory in western Java over the weekend, police have said.
The blaze broke out at a candy factory in the Serang Regency of Banten province at around 4:30 pm local time on Saturday, trapping workers inside. It had been extinguished by 6:30 am the following day.
Hendra Kurniawan, the chief inspector general of the Banten regional police force, said on Sunday that the bodies "were no longer physically identifiable" and that DNA testing would need to be used for identification purposes.
The presidential advisor for workers' welfare, Said Iqbal, said in a statement on Monday that the fire could have been caused by a short circuit in the building's AC system, but he stressed that further investigations were needed to determine how it began.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) shared footage on social media on Sunday showing emergency crews looking through the charred remains of the building.
Other images from the scene show extensive damage to the factory's roof as well as burned-out vehicles.
The candy company, Fonusa Agung Mulia, describes itself online as a subsidiary of Indonesia's UNIFAM food company.

Watch: Coughing, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
Police are investigating after thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester following an "unknown substance" being released into the crowd.
It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".
One woman was taken to hospital for treatment, while 88 other people were assessed by paramedics for "eye and respiratory symptoms".
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said detectives were trying to establish what the substance was and where it came from and further testing was taking place on items found at the venue.
A major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
The force said no arrests had yet been made and detectives were investigating "whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident".
GMP said 88 people underwent "dry decontamination at the scene" and were accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.
Some 12,000 people were evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue.
Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert.
A group of friends from Scunthorpe was standing in the mosh pit when the substance was released and said they "heard a pop" and "everyone coughing" and running away.
Molly, 19, said: "People not breathing, gagging, gasping for air. It was quite traumatic.
"People being wheeled out in wheelchairs covered in tinfoil, and no-one in the venue knew what was going on."
Kyan, 22, said: "When you breathed it in you tasted something weird. It didn't sit right - constant coughing, it sent a sting into your eyes."
The friends were later taken to the Etihad Stadium for the decontamination process.
Jack, 21, said some people had "pink liquid" on them and they were taken off to be tested.
"We were told to take off our clothes, and put on hazmat suits, slippers and a mask and taken to the Etihad to be observed," he said.
Charlie, 20, said he found the process a bit "invasive" and "confusing".
The friends said they were still suffering from symptoms, with a headache, chest pains and "really sore throat".
'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation
Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, say they were taken to the decontamination process
Joey Howe was at the gig and recalled the incident happening 30 or 40 minutes in.
The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.
Joey Howe says he wondered if it was "part of the show" until the smell hit
He said it was like "time stopped in motion" when "there was nothing going on".
"We then decided to go out. People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.
"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."
Howe also claimed security was "poor" and "very relaxed" with "people walking straight in".
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they had fled the venue.
The 23-year-old told the BBC that she went to the exit and saw lads on the bridge which leads into Medlock Square "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.
She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Concertgoers headed home after the performance was stopped by the incident
Malachi Clarke claimed security was "not good at all" at the venue.
The 19-year-old said: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
"Then we were told by a security guard it was chemical-related.
"After an hour or so of the gig being stopped, we were finally told to evacuate the venue."
Emergency services attended the Co-op Live arena in Manchester after a substance was let off in the crowd
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".
Harper, who was at the concert, told BBC Radio 5Live : "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.
"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.
"I saw people getting wheelchairs out...I was fearful it was something even worse."
Forensic officers are at the arena carrying out investigations
Fans at the rapper's other gigs have claimed similar incidents have taken place earlier on his tour.
They reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
Entrances to Co-op Live remain cordoned off, with police officers and security stewards manning the perimeter which is taped off.
Crime scene investigators in white protective overalls have been moving in and out of the building, as work continues to establish the nature of the substance that caused the evacuation.
The force said it was "an isolated incident" and there was "no wider threat to the public".
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk."
He added that more than 12,000 people had been "safely escorted" from the arena and thanked concertgoers for their "patience".
Harding urged anyone who left the event and had since become unwell to attend their local hospital.
Don Toliver recently received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy awards (file photo)
The ambulance service added: "Decontamination was carried out as a precaution and one patient was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment."
It said several crews attended, including the Hazardous Area Response Team.
Anyone who has since "noticed side-effects or become ill" is urged to seek medical advice.
There was a large police presence at the venue on Monday morning
In a statement, Co-op Live said venue bosses were working closely with police to identify the cause of the incident.
"Our priority remains the safety and security of all visitors to Co-op Live, and we will provide more information once we have an update from GMP," the statement said.
Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig said the major incident had now ended and she thanked emergency services and venue staff for their "professionalism".
"Enquiries into the cause of the incident are ongoing so those affected can get the answers they deserve," she added.
Toliver, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, was performing in Manchester as part of his Nitrous tour.
The 32-year-old musician has received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, including for Best New Artist.

US rapper Don Toliver has postponed his concert at London's O2 arena on Monday, a day after his Manchester show was evacuated after an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.
"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," he wrote on Instagram.
One person was taken to hospital and a total of 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.
Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
Watch: Coughs, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.
One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.
A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.
Joey Howe, a football journalist who was at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester he went into "panic mode" when he saw people running out of the venue.
He described a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."
Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.
"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."
Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".
Police investigate unknown substance that caused Manchester's Co-op Live evacuation
'People were screaming in pain' during Co-op Live evacuation
All fans at the Manchester show will get a full refund, promoter Live Nation said.
Postponing the O2 arena show, Live Nation blamed "production delays following last night's show at Co-op Live in Manchester".
A statement said: "We are sorry to everyone affected by last night's events in Manchester and full refunds for that show will be automatically processed to ticket holders."
There have apparently been similar incidents earlier on Toliver's tour, when some fans reported spray or gas being released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
In his post on Monday, the rapper said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night."
"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans," Toliver said, asking people to stop bringing substances into his shows.
"It ain't cool," added the rapper, who was nominated for five Grammy Awards earlier this month. "See you soon London, love you Guys. DT."
Toliver's Nitrous tour, named after his new album, is also due to visit Wembley Arena in London on Tuesday. No update has been given about that show.
It was set to be the last gig of his world tour before he took a break from the road ahead of a Coachella appearance next spring.
Toliver is best known for singles such as No Idea and After Party, from his debut studio album, Heaven or Hell (2020), which was big on TikTok. He also featured on Travis Scott's song Can't Say, from his third studio album Astroworld.

Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

Iran flogged pop singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her concert team on Monday following a December 2024 performance near Qom in which she sang without a hijab, her lawyer said.
Lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad news channel that the Qom prosecutor's office enforcement team carried out the sentence against Ahmadi in the early hours of Monday.
The flogging sentences against band members Sohail Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia, and concert organiser Mohsen Lashkari, were carried out on the same day, Nili said.
A criminal court in Qom province had sentenced nine members of the concert team to 74 lashes each, a two-year ban on leaving the country and a two-year ban on artistic activity.
The judiciary also sealed off the Deyr Gachin Caravanserai, the historic venue where the concert took place.
Ahmadi performed at the caravanserai near the historic city of Qom on the evening of 11 December 2024 without hijab. No audience was present.
The concert was broadcast live on YouTube and drew around 3 million views in the days that followed.
Ahmadi described the performance as a "hypothetical concert." Writing on her YouTube channel, she said, "I want to sing for the people I love. This is a right that I could not give up, that is, singing for the land that I love passionately."
The criminal court of Qom charged the group with "offending public decency by producing and disseminating vulgar and immoral content online."
Amnesty International called in June for the sentences to be quashed, saying flogging was "a cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment" that violated the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill-treatment.
The organisation called on Tehran to abolish compulsory veiling and corporal punishment and to end the criminalisation of freedom of expression.
Under Islamic Republic law, women are banned from singing in public in spaces where men are present.
Although criminal law does not explicitly criminalise women's singing as such, female performers typically face charges of encouraging corruption and prostitution, failing to observe hijab, or offending public decency.
Authorities have used the charge in recent years to close many Instagram pages belonging to Iranian female singers. Appearing in public without hijab is punishable by between 10 days and two months in prison, up to 74 lashes or a fine.
The sentences against Ahmadi and her collaborators stand in contrast to scenes from pro-government rallies held during the US and Israeli military strikes on Iran earlier in 2026, when images circulated widely showing women at the gatherings without mandatory hijab.
A performance by Lebanese singer Julia Boutros was also broadcast at a pro-government gathering in Tehran, where Boutros also did not wear hijab.
Earlier, during the Woman, Life, Freedom protest movement in 2022, Ahmadi had performed the protest song "Az khun-e javanan-e vatan" or "From the blood of the nation's youths".
After it was widely shared on social media, her home was searched by security forces and she was ordered to report to the security prosecutor's office in Tehran.
The Woman, Life, Freedom movement emerged in Iran in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, 21, in the custody of Tehran's morality police. Amini had been detained over alleged issues with her hijab.
Human rights organisations say the subsequent crackdown left more than 500 people dead.

India has offered Nepal a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees (€1.4 billion) to help it recover from the catastrophic floods that tore through the Himalayan country in August.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the announcement in New Delhi, India, on Monday, standing alongside his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah.
"We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August," Modi said.
"To support Nepal's reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees (€1.4 billion)," he added.
New Delhi did not immediately say what the package would include. Nepal estimates the total cost of reconstruction at €4.35 billion.
His call came a day after the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, collapsed without a deal, when the EU and other countries rejected a final text that made no mention of fossil fuels.
The 26 August disaster began with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly.
Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.
More than 1,400 people were killed and 5,000 left missing . In the days after the disaster, at least 900 workers were reported missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the floods.
The scale of the death toll overwhelmed morgues and forensic teams.
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, produces only a tiny share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Shah said the disaster showed the "imperative to address the challenges of climate change through collective action".
In October, the United Nations' climate loss and damage fund approved $20 million (€18.2m) for Nepal. That is the most a country can request in a single application, and it was the first money the fund had set aside for any nation.
"Our commitment will be to help affected families rebuild their lives, create new opportunities and further strengthen Nepal's capacity to deal with future disasters," Modi said.
